Welcome to **Two-Nil**! This is the first post on the blog, where I'll publish
football data analyses, mostly in R.

To kick things off, there's no better question than the one that gives the
blog its name: **what is the probability of a match ending 2–0?**

## A simple model

A classic starting point is to assume that each team's goals follow a Poisson
distribution, independent of the opponent, with a mean equal to that team's
expected goals (xG) in the match.

Let's imagine a match where the home side has an xG of 1.6 and the away side,
1.1.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggplot2)
source(here::here("R/theme_two_nil.R"))

xg_home <- 1.6
xg_away <- 1.1
max_goals <- 5

scorelines <- expand.grid(
  home = 0:max_goals,
  away = 0:max_goals
)
scorelines$prob <- dpois(scorelines$home, xg_home) *
  dpois(scorelines$away, xg_away)
```

The probability of a 2–0 home win is:

```{r}
#| label: prob-2-0
p_2_0 <- with(scorelines, prob[home == 2 & away == 0])
scales::percent(p_2_0, accuracy = 0.1)
```

## Every scoreline

```{r}
#| label: fig-scorelines
#| fig-cap: "Probability of each scoreline with an xG of 1.6 (home) and 1.1 (away)."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggplot(scorelines, aes(away, home, fill = prob)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = scales::percent(prob, accuracy = 0.1)),
    size = 3.2,
    colour = ifelse(scorelines$prob > 0.08, "white", "grey20")
  ) +
  annotate(
    "tile", x = 0, y = 2, width = 1, height = 1,
    fill = NA, colour = two_nil_colors[["ink"]], linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = two_nil_colors[["chalk"]], high = two_nil_colors[["pitch"]], guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:max_goals, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:max_goals, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "What are the odds of each scoreline?",
    x = "Away goals",
    y = "Home goals",
    caption = "Independent Poisson model. Highlighted: 2–0."
  ) +
  theme_two_nil() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

This model ignores a lot (correlation between the two teams' goals, game
state, the fact that low scores are more common than Poisson predicts…), but
it's a great starting point. In the next posts, the plan is to use real data
and make the analyses progressively more sophisticated.

See you next time!
